cases.presenting_complaint: Hearing voices commenting on my actions, believing people are following me, and feeling that TV is sending me messages for 3 months
cases.associated: Third-person auditory hallucinations (running commentary), persecutory delusions (MI5 surveillance), ideas of reference (TV/radio have special messages for him), social withdrawal, poor self-care, stopped attending university, cannabis use
cases.risk_factors: Family history of schizophrenia in uncle, cannabis use since age 16, recent academic stress, social isolation, prodrome of 6 months (social withdrawal, odd beliefs)
cases.mse: Appearance: Unkempt, poor hygiene, suspicious. Behavior: Guarded, checking windows/doors. Speech: Normal rate but content abnormal. Mood: 'They're after me'. Affect: Flat, incongruous smiling. Thought: Persecutory delusions, ideas of reference, thought broadcast. Perception: Third-person auditory hallucinations (running commentary). Cognition: Distracted by hallucinations. Insight: Absent
cases.investigations: Urine drug screen: Cannabis positive. MRI brain: No acute pathology. Blood: Normal metabolic panel, TSH. PANSS (Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale): High positive symptoms score
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate-high risk. Command hallucinations (check content), paranoia may lead to self-harm, increased risk in first episode psychosis
cases.explanation: First Episode Psychosis: initial presentation of psychotic symptoms. Schizophrenia diagnosis requires ≥2 of 5 symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized behavior, negative symptoms) with ≥1 being delusions/hallucinations/disorganized speech, ≥6 months duration including prodrome. This patient has 3 positive symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, negative symptoms emerging). Critical period: early intervention in first 5 years improves prognosis dramatically. Cannabis use may have precipitated in vulnerable individual
cases.management: URGENT: (1) Psychiatric admission if high risk or no insight; (2) Comprehensive assessment - exclude organic causes, substance-induced; (3) Antipsychotic medication: Start atypical (risperidone 2-4mg, olanzapine 10-15mg, aripiprazole 10-15mg - lower doses in first episode); (4) Benzodiazepines PRN for agitation; (5) Monitor for side effects closely in first episode; (6) Early Intervention in Psychosis (EIP) service referral - specialized team for first episode. ACUTE: (7) Psychoeducation (when settled) about psychosis and schizophrenia; (8) Family intervention; (9) Stop cannabis use - strongly associated with worse outcomes; (10) Address university - medical leave, potential to return. ONGOING: (11) CBT for psychosis; (12) Social and occupational recovery; (13) Monitor for depression post-psychosis; (14) Long-term antipsychotic (2-5 years minimum); (15) Regular monitoring; (16) Relapse prevention. Prognosis better if first episode treated promptly

cases.presenting_complaint: Long-standing beliefs that neighbors are trying to poison him through walls, hearing multiple voices arguing about him for 15 years
cases.associated: Persistent auditory hallucinations (multiple voices discussing him in third person, some command hallucinations), systematized paranoid delusions (elaborate plot by neighbors involving radiation through walls), negative symptoms (social withdrawal, poor motivation, flat affect), poor medication adherence
cases.risk_factors: Schizophrenia diagnosed age 27, multiple psychiatric admissions (8 admissions), medication non-adherence, limited social support, lives alone, unemployed on disability
cases.mse: Appearance: Disheveled, malodorous. Behavior: Suspicious, guarded. Speech: Circumstantial. Mood: 'The neighbors won't leave me alone'. Affect: Flat, blunted. Thought: Fixed systematized paranoid delusions, some loosening of associations. Perception: Persistent auditory hallucinations. Cognition: Some impairment. Insight: Absent
cases.investigations: Previous imaging: Mild ventricular enlargement (typical of chronic schizophrenia). Current medication: Olanzapine prescribed but not taking regularly. Depot consideration needed
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk. Command hallucinations, chronic illness with multiple admissions, social isolation, impaired judgment
cases.explanation: Chronic schizophrenia with poor outcome: characterized by persistent positive symptoms (delusions, hallucinations) plus prominent negative symptoms and functional decline despite treatment. Paranoid type: dominated by persecutory delusions. Poor prognostic factors: male sex, insidious onset, prominent negative symptoms, poor social function premorbid, medication non-adherence, substance use. Treatment resistance and multiple relapses indicate need for different approach
cases.management: (1) Assess current risk and need for admission; (2) Address medication non-adherence: switch to long-acting injectable (LAI) antipsychotic - paliperidone palmitate monthly, risperidone LAI bi-weekly, or aripiprazole monohydrate monthly (avoids daily compliance issue); (3) Consider clozapine if treatment-resistant (failed 2 adequate trials); (4) Clozapine requires registration, weekly bloods initially; (5) Assertive Community Treatment (ACT) team for intensive support; (6) Address social determinants: housing quality, financial support, disability benefits; (7) CBT for psychosis targeting delusions; (8) Cognitive remediation for cognitive impairment; (9) Vocational rehabilitation - supported employment if stable; (10) Family education if family contact exists; (11) Monitor physical health (high rates of metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease in chronic schizophrenia); (12) Address negative symptoms (often most disabling) - social inclusion, activity scheduling; (13) Long-term case management; (14) Realistic goals - stabilization and improved quality of life rather than full remission

cases.presenting_complaint: Sudden onset of hearing God's voice, believing she has special powers, and bizarre behavior for 5 days following death of her mother
cases.associated: Auditory hallucinations (God's voice telling her mother is watching her), grandiose delusions (has special healing powers), disorganized behavior (trying to 'heal' strangers on street, giving away possessions), marked distress, no previous psychiatric history
cases.risk_factors: Acute severe stressor (mother's sudden death 6 days ago), no psychiatric history, no substance use, previously well-functioning
cases.mse: Appearance: Disheveled, wearing unusual combination of clothing. Behavior: Disorganized, intrusive, attempting to touch examiner to 'heal'. Speech: Pressured, tangential. Mood: 'Blessed, mother sent me mission'. Affect: Labile, inappropriate. Thought: Grandiose and religious delusions. Perception: Auditory hallucinations (God's voice). Cognition: Disoriented to situation. Insight: Absent
cases.investigations: Urine drug screen: Negative. Blood: Normal. MRI brain: Normal. Collateral history: Previously high-functioning, no psychiatric history. Clear stressor (mother's death) precipitated symptoms
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk. Impaired judgment, potential for risky behavior, acute grief underlying presentation
cases.explanation: Brief Psychotic Disorder: presence of ≥1 of delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, or grossly disorganized/catatonic behavior, lasting ≥1 day but <1 month, with eventual return to premorbid functioning. Specifier: 'with marked stressor' (death of mother). Distinguishable from schizophrenia by brief duration and full return to baseline. Better prognosis than schizophrenia - 50-80% do not develop chronic psychotic disorder. Important to exclude substance-induced, medical causes, mood disorder with psychotic features
cases.management: ACUTE: (1) Psychiatric admission for safety and assessment; (2) Low-stimulation environment; (3) Supportive care; (4) Short-term antipsychotic (low dose risperidone 1-2mg or olanzapine 5-10mg); (5) Benzodiazepines for agitation/distress (lorazepam 1-2mg PRN); (6) Monitor daily - symptoms should improve within days to 1-2 weeks; (7) Exclude ongoing medical/substance causes. ACUTE PHASE: (8) Supportive psychotherapy; (9) Allow grieving process once psychosis resolves; (10) Family support and psychoeducation. RECOVERY: (11) Taper antipsychotic after 1-2 weeks of stability (brief treatment only - not long-term); (12) Bereavement counseling; (13) Psychoeducation about stressor-induced psychosis; (14) Follow-up for 6-12 months to monitor for recurrence; (15) Address grief; (16) Excellent prognosis for this episode but 20-50% risk of recurrence with future severe stressors; (17) Relapse prevention - identify early warning signs for future stressors

cases.presenting_complaint: Seeing shadow people, believing police are surveilling him through electronics, extreme paranoia for 2 weeks during methamphetamine binge
cases.associated: Visual hallucinations (shadow figures, insects crawling on skin), auditory hallucinations (footsteps, whispers), severe paranoia (police surveillance, believes phones/computers are bugged), tactile hallucinations (formication - bugs under skin), aggressive behavior, insomnia (awake 5 days straight)
cases.risk_factors: Methamphetamine use disorder (IV use, 2g/day for 2 weeks), previous similar episodes always related to meth use, symptom-free when abstinent (had 6 month abstinent period last year with no psychiatric symptoms)
cases.mse: Appearance: Unkempt, poor dentition, skin picking lesions, appears older than age. Behavior: Agitated, hypervigilant, checking windows. Speech: Rapid, pressured. Mood: 'They're coming for me'. Affect: Fearful, hostile. Thought: Paranoid delusions (police surveillance), ideas of reference. Perception: Visual (shadow people), auditory (footsteps), and tactile (formication) hallucinations. Cognition: Inattentive. Insight: Absent
cases.investigations: Urine drug screen: Positive for methamphetamine and amphetamine. Tachycardia 120bpm, hypertension 160/100. Pupils dilated. Timeline: Symptoms began day 3 of binge, escalated with continued use. Previous notes document complete resolution with abstinence
cases.suicide_risk: High risk. Paranoia may lead to impulsive violence (toward self or others - perceived threats), impaired judgment, agitation, stimulant crash depression follows
cases.explanation: Methamphetamine-Induced Psychotic Disorder: psychotic symptoms caused by stimulant intoxication exceeding typical intoxication effects. Methamphetamine causes massive dopamine release leading to psychosis. Classic features: visual hallucinations (esp shadow people), formication (bugs under skin leading to skin-picking), paranoia, insomnia. Symptoms typically resolve within days to weeks of cessation but can persist longer. Distinguished from primary psychosis by: temporal relationship with use, specific symptom profile (visual and tactile hallucinations uncommon in schizophrenia), resolution with abstinence, no symptoms during previous abstinent periods. ~10% of meth users develop psychosis, risk increases with dose and duration
cases.management: ACUTE EMERGENCY: (1) Ensure safety - may be violent if paranoid; (2) Calm environment, reduce stimulation; (3) Medical stabilization: monitor vitals (hypertension, tachycardia, hyperthermia), IV fluids, check for rhabdomyolysis; (4) Benzodiazepines for agitation and autonomic symptoms (lorazepam 2-4mg, repeat as needed); (5) Antipsychotic for severe psychosis (haloperidol 5mg IM or olanzapine 10mg IM, though benzodiazepines often preferred initially); (6) Address skin-picking injuries. ACUTE PHASE: (7) Observation - symptoms typically improve over 3-7 days of abstinence; (8) Sleep hygiene - recovery requires sleep; (9) Nutrition. ONGOING: (10) Substance use treatment (PRIMARY): residential rehab vs intensive outpatient; (11) Motivational interviewing; (12) Contingency management (effective for stimulants); (13) Treat comorbid disorders; (14) DISCONTINUE antipsychotic once symptoms resolve (do not treat long-term if substance-induced); (15) Monitor for stimulant withdrawal depression (severe - high suicide risk); (16) Peer support (NA, SMART Recovery); (17) Address social determinants; (18) High relapse risk - long-term recovery support; (19) Psychoeducation - meth neurotoxicity, risk of chronic cognitive impairment

cases.presenting_complaint: Acute confusion, seeing deceased relatives in the room, believing he's in a hotel not hospital, for 2 days post-hip surgery
cases.associated: Fluctuating consciousness (alert morning, confused evening), disorientation to time and place, visual hallucinations (seeing deceased wife), delusions (believes in hotel), agitation especially night (sundowning), inattention, disturbed sleep-wake cycle, picking at bedsheets
cases.risk_factors: Post-operative day 2 (hip fracture repair), age 76, polypharmacy (8 medications), poor pain control (receiving opioids), dehydration, urinary catheter, previous mild cognitive impairment
cases.mse: Appearance: In hospital gown, appears distressed. Behavior: Agitated, attempting to remove IV lines, picking at sheets. Speech: Incoherent at times. Mood: Cannot assess. Affect: Fearful. Thought: Disorganized, persecutory ideas (staff trying to harm him). Perception: Visual hallucinations (wife at bedside). Cognition: Disoriented to time and place, inattentive, waxing-waning. Insight: Absent
cases.investigations: CAM (Confusion Assessment Method): Positive for delirium. Workup: CXR (query aspiration), urine C&S (UTI), FBC (infection), metabolic panel (electrolytes), medication review (opioids, anticholinergics), pain assessment. CT head: Old infarcts, no acute pathology
cases.suicide_risk: Low for suicide but high risk of harm (falls, pulling lines, aggression)
cases.explanation: Delirium: acute confusional state characterized by disturbance in attention/awareness and cognition, develops acutely (hours-days), fluctuates, and is due to medical condition. Psychotic features (hallucinations, delusions) common in delirium but are NOT primary psychotic disorder. Key distinguishing features from primary psychosis: acute onset, fluctuating course, inattention, disorientation, medical context (post-op), older age. Risk factors: age >65, dementia, surgery, medications (opioids, benzodiazepines, anticholinergics), infections, metabolic disturbance. Hyperactive subtype shown here (also hypoactive and mixed). Emergency - requires medical treatment of underlying cause
cases.management: TREAT UNDERLYING CAUSE (PRIMARY): (1) Comprehensive workup: infection (UTI, pneumonia, wound), metabolic (electrolytes, glucose, renal, liver), medications (stop/reduce opioids, anticholinergics), pain (inadequate pain worsens delirium), hypoxia, constipation, urinary retention; (2) Remove urinary catheter if possible; (3) Treat identified causes (antibiotics for UTI, correct electrolytes, hydration). NON-PHARMACOLOGICAL (FIRST-LINE): (4) Reorientation (clocks, calendars, family photos); (5) Frequent verbal reorientation; (6) Minimize room changes; (7) Restore sleep-wake cycle (lights on during day, minimize nighttime disruption); (8) Mobilize early; (9) Glasses and hearing aids; (10) Familiar family members present; (11) Avoid restraints (worsen agitation). PHARMACOLOGICAL (only if non-pharm fails and patient safety risk): (12) Low-dose antipsychotic (haloperidol 0.5-1mg PO/IM or quetiapine 25mg) - use lowest dose, shortest duration; (13) Avoid benzodiazepines (worsen delirium except in alcohol withdrawal); (14) Discontinue as soon as delirium resolves. PROGNOSIS: Usually resolves with treatment of underlying cause but may take days-weeks. Delirium increases mortality and risk of institutionalization

cases.presenting_complaint: Firm belief that coworkers are conspiring to get her fired, has lodged multiple complaints against them over past 2 years
cases.associated: Single, non-bizarre delusion (coworker conspiracy to sabotage her work and reputation). No hallucinations, no other psychotic symptoms. Otherwise functioning normally in other life domains. Has made numerous complaints to HR, consulted lawyers, installed security cameras at home. Behavior logical within delusional framework
cases.risk_factors: Late onset (age 52), social isolation, no family history of psychosis, difficult workplace relationships, underlying personality traits (suspicious, rigid)
cases.mse: Appearance: Professional, well-groomed. Behavior: Cooperative but guarded when discussing coworkers. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'Angry about the injustice'. Affect: Restricted, irritable. Thought: Single non-bizarre systematized delusion (workplace conspiracy), otherwise logical thought process. Perception: No hallucinations. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Absent regarding delusion, otherwise good
cases.investigations: No substance use. Medical workup: Normal. Collateral from workplace: No evidence of conspiracy, patient performance adequate, multiple unfounded complaints filed. No other psychiatric symptoms. Personality assessment: Paranoid traits
cases.suicide_risk: Low-moderate risk. If delusion leads to job loss, risk increases due to loss and perceived persecution
cases.explanation: Delusional Disorder: presence of ≥1 delusions for ≥1 month, criteria for schizophrenia never met (no prominent hallucinations, no disorganized speech/behavior, minimal negative symptoms), functioning not markedly impaired except directly related to delusion, mood episodes brief if present. Persecutory type: delusion that individual being conspired against. Key features: delusion is non-bizarre (could potentially occur - workplace conspiracy is possible, unlike aliens), encapsulated (doesn't spread to other domains), functioning otherwise intact. Rare disorder (0.2% prevalence). Often presents late (40s-50s). Differential: paranoid personality disorder (no frank delusions), schizophrenia (other symptoms present), psychotic depression (mood symptoms prominent)
cases.management: CHALLENGING DISORDER TO TREAT: (1) Engagement crucial - patient unlikely to seek help voluntarily, doesn't believe ill; (2) Build therapeutic alliance - don't directly challenge delusion initially but explore impact on life; (3) Antipsychotic medication: evidence limited but may help - atypical antipsychotic (risperidone 2-4mg, olanzapine 10mg) but often refused; (4) CBT for delusions: don't aim to eliminate belief but reduce distress and impact - explore evidence, consider alternative explanations, improve coping; (5) Assess risk to others (anger at coworkers - potential for violence?); (6) Social interventions: is workplace change possible? Though may recreate delusion in new setting; (7) Treat comorbid depression/anxiety if present; (8) Address isolation - social engagement; (9) Family therapy if available; (10) Monitor closely - may escalate (litigation, confrontation, violence). PROGNOSIS: Often chronic, waxing-waning. Some stabilize over time. Rarely full remission. Key is minimizing impact on functioning

cases.presenting_complaint: Believes that government is monitoring family through smart meters and has moved in with sister who initially developed this belief 5 years ago
cases.associated: Sister (primary case) has long-standing paranoid schizophrenia with persecutory delusions about government surveillance. Patient (secondary case) was initially skeptical but after moving in with sister 18 months ago has adopted identical delusional system. Both have disconnected electricity, use candles, avoid all electronics. Patient has no other psychotic symptoms, no hallucinations
cases.risk_factors: Lives with psychotic sister (dominant partner), socially isolated (only contact is sister), financially dependent on sister, no previous psychiatric history, left job to move in with sister
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriate. Behavior: Cooperative but suspicious about examiner's intentions. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'Worried about government surveillance'. Affect: Anxious, appropriate. Thought: Shared delusion with sister (government monitoring through smart meters), otherwise logical. Perception: No hallucinations. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Absent regarding delusion
cases.investigations: Assessment confirms sister has chronic schizophrenia. Patient's delusion temporally related to moving in with sister. No evidence of primary psychotic disorder in patient. No hallucinations, no thought disorder, functioning would be normal if separated
cases.suicide_risk: Low risk in patient. Primary case (sister) may have higher risk
cases.explanation: Shared Psychotic Disorder (Folie à Deux): delusional belief develops in individual in context of close relationship with another person with established delusion. The induced person (secondary) adopts the delusional belief system of the primary person. Rare disorder. Typical pattern: dominant partner (often with schizophrenia or delusional disorder) influences submissive partner who is socially isolated and dependent. Delusion in secondary case is typically less fixed and resolves with separation from primary case. Must meet: secondary person has no other psychotic symptoms, delusion develops in context of relationship, delusion identical or very similar to primary case
cases.management: (1) SEPARATION is key intervention - separate patient from sister (primary case); (2) Hospitalization of patient may be necessary to achieve separation; (3) Once separated, induced delusion typically resolves within weeks to months without antipsychotic medication; (4) Psychotherapy for patient: understand relationship dynamics, build independent identity, address dependency; (5) Social support and housing for patient (prevent return to sister); (6) If delusion doesn't resolve after separation, reconsider diagnosis (may be independent delusional disorder or schizophrenia); (7) Treat primary case (sister): antipsychotic optimization, case management; (8) Family therapy involving both if appropriate and safe; (9) Address patient's isolation and dependency issues; (10) Vocational rehabilitation - return to work; (11) Build independent social network; (12) Maintain separation long-term (may need to prevent contact initially); (13) Monitor for relapse if contact resumed. PROGNOSIS: Good for secondary case if separation maintained. Primary case prognosis depends on underlying disorder (likely chronic in schizophrenia)

cases.presenting_complaint: Current manic episode with grandiose delusions and hallucinations, history of psychotic episodes even when mood is normal
cases.duration: Current episode 2 weeks, illness for 8 years
cases.associated: Current: manic symptoms (elevated mood, decreased sleep, grandiosity) PLUS psychotic symptoms (grandiose delusions that he's a prophet, auditory hallucinations - God's voice). History: has had major mood episodes (manic and depressive) WITH psychosis, but crucially also has periods where psychotic symptoms persist without mood symptoms
cases.risk_factors: Family history of both bipolar disorder (mother) and schizophrenia (paternal uncle), cannabis use, multiple psychiatric admissions (6), poor medication adherence
cases.mse: Appearance: Flamboyant clothing, religious jewelry. Behavior: Overactive, pressured. Speech: Pressured, tangential. Mood: 'Blessed, spreading God's message'. Affect: Elevated, expansive. Thought: Grandiose delusions (believes he is a prophet), religious preoccupation, flight of ideas. Perception: Auditory hallucinations (God giving him commands). Cognition: Distractible. Insight: Absent
cases.investigations: Longitudinal history review: Previous episodes include (1) psychosis without mood symptoms for 3 months; (2) major depression with psychosis; (3) mania with psychosis. Critical: psychosis persists beyond mood episodes. Current: urine drug screen positive for cannabis. PANSS and YMRS both elevated
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate-high risk. Schizoaffective disorder has high suicide risk (similar to schizophrenia). Impulsivity from mania, command hallucinations increase risk
cases.explanation: Schizoaffective Disorder: meets criteria for major mood episode (manic or depressive) concurrent with criteria A for schizophrenia (delusions, hallucinations, etc), AND delusions/hallucinations for ≥2 weeks in absence of major mood episode during lifetime duration of illness, AND mood symptoms present for majority of illness. Difficult diagnosis requiring longitudinal perspective. Bipolar type: has had manic episodes. Distinguishing features: from Bipolar with psychotic features (psychosis ONLY during mood episodes), from Schizophrenia (mood symptoms are NOT prominent/majority of illness). This diagnosis is intermediate between schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Controversial diagnosis - diagnostic reliability moderate. Functional impairment between schizophrenia and bipolar
cases.management: COMBINATION TREATMENT (mood + psychosis): (1) Mood stabilizer (lithium or valproate) PLUS antipsychotic - combination is essential; (2) For current manic episode: antipsychotic with mood stabilizing properties (olanzapine 15-20mg, quetiapine 400-600mg, asenapine, cariprazine) OR lithium/valproate PLUS antipsychotic (risperidone, aripiprazole); (3) Benzodiazepines PRN for agitation; (4) Admission if high risk or poor support. ACUTE PHASE: (5) Monitor for switch to depression (common post-mania); (6) Address substance use (cannabis cessation critical). MAINTENANCE (CRUCIAL - prevent relapse): (7) Long-term combination therapy - mood stabilizer PLUS antipsychetic; (8) Some patients stable on antipsychotic monotherapy (quetiapine, lurasidone, cariprazine have mood and psychosis efficacy); (9) Consider long-acting injectable if adherence poor; (10) Psychoeducation about lifelong illness; (11) Family psychoeducation; (12) CBT for psychosis; (13) Social and vocational rehabilitation; (14) Monitoring: mood, psychosis, side effects, substance use; (15) Early warning sign identification; (16) Long-term case management. PROGNOSIS: Intermediate between schizophrenia (worse) and bipolar disorder (better). Better functional outcomes than schizophrenia but worse than bipolar disorder

cases.presenting_complaint: Severe depression with beliefs that body is rotting inside, hearing voices telling her she deserves to die for 6 weeks
cases.associated: Severe depressive symptoms: profound anhedonia, psychomotor retardation, early morning wakening, weight loss (8kg), pervasive guilt. Psychotic symptoms: nihilistic delusion (Cotard's syndrome - believes body is rotting, organs failing, already dead), mood-congruent auditory hallucinations (voice telling her she's worthless and should die), guilt about past minor mistakes
cases.risk_factors: Previous depressive episodes but never psychotic, age 63 (late-onset psychosis concerning), social isolation (husband died 2 years ago), medical comorbidity (hypertension, diabetes)
cases.mse: Appearance: Unkempt, poor self-care, appears ill. Behavior: Severe psychomotor retardation. Speech: Minimal, long latency, monotone. Mood: 'Dead inside, rotting away'. Affect: Flat, depressed. Thought: Nihilistic delusions (believes organs have stopped working, is dead), guilt, self-blame, active suicidal ideation. Perception: Auditory hallucinations (voice telling her to die). Cognition: Impaired by depression. Insight: Absent
cases.investigations: PHQ-9: 27/27 (severe depression). Medical workup: No evidence of organic disease causing symptoms (comprehensive metabolic panel normal). Previous records: two prior depressive episodes, both non-psychotic, responded to SSRIs. Current episode much more severe
cases.suicide_risk: VERY HIGH RISK. Psychotic depression has very high suicide risk - delusions create hopelessness, auditory hallucinations commanding self-harm, severe depression, social isolation, older age, widow. IMMEDIATE intervention required
cases.explanation: Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features: major depressive episode with delusions and/or hallucinations. Psychotic features are typically mood-congruent (themes of guilt, punishment, nihilism, disease, death) but can be incongruent. Seen in ~15% of severe depressions. More common with increasing age. Cotard's syndrome: nihilistic delusion that one is dead or body parts are decaying - classic of psychotic depression. This is psychiatric emergency due to high suicide risk (30-50% attempt suicide). Poor response to antidepressants alone - requires antipsychotic. ECT highly effective. Must distinguish from schizoaffective (this has no psychosis outside depression) and schizophrenia (no prominent mood symptoms)
cases.management: PSYCHIATRIC EMERGENCY: (1) Urgent psychiatric admission (involuntary if refuses and suicidal); (2) Close observation (one-to-one if high risk); (3) Remove means for self-harm. PHARMACOLOGICAL: (4) Antidepressant PLUS antipsychotic combination is essential (neither alone sufficient): SSRI/SNRI (sertraline 150-200mg, venlafaxine 225-375mg) PLUS antipsychotic (olanzapine 10-20mg, quetiapine 200-400mg, aripiprazole 10-15mg); (5) Consider ECT as first-line treatment (highly effective for psychotic depression, faster response than medications, may be life-saving) - especially given high suicide risk and older age; (6) If ECT: bilateral electrode placement, 6-12 sessions typically. ACUTE PHASE: (7) Daily assessments; (8) Gradual introduction of activities; (9) Nutritional support (weight loss); (10) Medical monitoring (diabetes, hypertension). CONTINUATION: (11) Continue combination therapy 6-12 months after remission; (12) Can attempt antipsychotic taper but many relapse - some need long-term; (13) Psychotherapy when less depressed; (14) Bereavement work (husband's death); (15) Social re-engagement; (16) Long-term antidepressant (high relapse risk, psychotic episode is poor prognostic sign); (17) Close monitoring for relapse. PROGNOSIS: Good response to ECT/combination therapy but high recurrence risk

cases.presenting_complaint: Stopped moving, speaking, eating and drinking for 3 days, maintaining unusual postures, brought in by family
cases.associated: Catatonic features: mutism (not speaking), stupor (decreased responsiveness), waxy flexibility (maintains imposed postures), posturing (odd positions), negativism (opposes examiner), staring. Underlying schizophrenia (diagnosed 5 years ago, recently stopped medications). Family reports gradual decline over 2 weeks before complete shutdown
cases.risk_factors: Known schizophrenia, medication non-adherence (stopped antipsychotic 1 month ago), previous catatonic episode 3 years ago responded to lorazepam
cases.mse: Appearance: Immobile, maintains unusual posture with arm raised. Behavior: Catatonic - no spontaneous movement, mute, maintains imposed postures (waxy flexibility), staring. Speech: Mute. Mood: Cannot assess. Affect: Immobile, blank expression. Thought: Cannot assess. Perception: Cannot assess. Cognition: Cannot assess due to lack of response. Insight: Cannot assess
cases.investigations: Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale: 22/69 (catatonia confirmed). Medical workup: CK mildly elevated (from immobility), otherwise normal labs. ECG: normal. CT head: no acute pathology. Lorazepam challenge test: 2mg IV lorazepam results in temporary improvement (diagnostic and therapeutic). Temperature normal (exclude NMS)
cases.suicide_risk: Unable to assess but catatonia itself is medical emergency (risk of death from complications: dehydration, DVT, aspiration, rhabdomyolysis)
cases.explanation: Catatonia: psychomotor syndrome characterized by ≥3 of: catalepsy, waxy flexibility, stupor, agitation, mutism, negativism, posturing, mannerisms, stereotypies, grimacing, echolalia, echopraxia. Can occur in: schizophrenia (10-15%), mood disorders (depression or mania), medical conditions, medications. This is catatonia secondary to schizophrenia exacerbation (after stopping meds). Medical emergency: complications include DVT, pneumonia, pressure ulcers, rhabdomyolysis, dehydration, death. Requires urgent treatment. Lorazepam challenge: 1-2mg IV lorazepam leads to temporary improvement in 60-80% - both diagnostic and therapeutic
cases.management: MEDICAL EMERGENCY: (1) Admit to medical/psychiatric unit with close monitoring; (2) Medical stabilization: IV fluids (dehydration), nutrition (NG tube if needed), DVT prophylaxis (heparin), monitor vitals and CK (rhabdomyolysis), prevent pressure ulcers (turning), aspiration precautions; (3) Lorazepam (FIRST-LINE treatment): 1-2mg IV/IM test dose, then 2mg TDS, increase up to 8-16mg/day in divided doses. Response typically within 48-72 hours; (4) If no response to lorazepam: ELECTROCONVULSIVE THERAPY (ECT) - highly effective for catatonia, often dramatic response, 6-10 bilateral treatments; (5) Restart antipsychotic once able to take PO (catatonia related to schizophrenia relapse) - BUT caution: antipsychotics can worsen catatonia, start low dose, continue lorazepam; (6) Consider long-acting injectable antipsychotic to prevent future non-adherence; (7) Monitor for neuroleptic malignant syndrome (fever, rigidity, elevated CK, autonomic instability) - life-threatening, requires immediate intervention if occurs; (8) Physical therapy once improving. ONGOING: (9) Identify trigger (medication non-adherence); (10) Medication adherence interventions; (11) Family education; (12) Early warning signs; (13) Maintenance lorazepam may be needed in some patients prone to catatonia. PROGNOSIS: Generally good response to treatment (lorazepam or ECT) but can recur
